transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the plank toll-post where the Ashwater Causeway narrows to a single slick rail above black water. A Warden lantern-boy chalks names on a slate nobody can read in this downpour, and behind him the causeway itself groans, half-swallowed already at its southern end. You four end up shoulder to shoulder in the queue — strangers, or near enough — each staring south toward Gullet Ford, each aware the water is a finger higher than it was this morning and climbing. Somewhere out past the reeds, faint as a fever dream, a chain drags across sunken stone, and no one wants to say out loud what that sound might mean.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: She doesn't look at the others yet, just speaks low enough that only the closest will hear over the rain: "That water's climbing fast—faster than it should. And whatever's dragging that chain down there, it's not the weather doing it alone."

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde stands among the strangers, rain streaming down her weathered face, and her eyes track the black water with the focused calm of someone who's lived on it for years. Her hands work together unconsciously—the same rhythm as kneading bread—and she leans slightly into the spray, watching how the current breaks against the causeway's supports. That chain sound reaches her ears and she stiffens almost imperceptibly. She knows that note. She's heard it before in deep water, in places where things best left alone had been left alone.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: The water remembers. That chain sound... I've heard it before, and nothing good comes after.

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous stands motionless at the rail, hands gripping the slick wood as he stares down at the black water churning barely a man's-length below. The rain hammers cold against his face, and he watches the patterns it makes on the dark surface with the intense focus of someone reading omens. When that chain sound reaches him again—dragging, inevitable—his fingers twitch against the wet wood.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: That's no river sound. The hive-touched are in the deep water, and they're moving toward us. We don't have the luxury of waiting for the tide—we either cross now or we fight.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (I push through the crowd toward the railing, ignoring the Warden's protests. That dragging chain sound cuts through the rain like a blade. I've heard it before—in the ruins after the first outbreak, in the empty halls where the hive-touched were herded like cattle. I close my eyes and listen, letting my knowledge of the afflicted speak to me. That's iron on stone, and something bound and furious dragging it forward.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Something in my bones says that's not just water moving past sunken stone—that's intent, that's movement. Whatever's out there, it knows we're here.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire leans against the causeway rail, narrowing her eyes toward the sound echoing across the dark water. Her hand rests near her weapon as she tries to piece together what's making that noise—something heavy and deliberate, something with weight and purpose. Every watch drill, every year holding the line, teaches you to read threat in the details.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: No—the water, that chain sound, it remembers I survived the Barge, and now it's calling me back under—my hands won't let go and I can't breathe—

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Aldous's knuckles go white on the rail as the chain-drag needles into an old wound — for one long breath he's back on the Sunken Barge, water closing over his head, and it takes Ysolde's hand on his shoulder to pull him back into the rain and the queue. Morwen closes her eyes and lets the sound speak to her the way the ruins once did: that's not current on stone, that's iron dragged by something bound and straining against its own weight — chains, and whatever wears them is still moving. Mire reads the same water with a Warden's eye for threat and confirms it: the drag has rhythm, purpose, intent behind it, not the blind push of flood. Between them they've turned a formless dread into something nameable — the party now knows, with certainty, that something bound is dragging itself toward the causeway, and it means to reach them before the water does.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: You're back here now, not under. Breathe. Whatever took you down before, we're not going alone this time—and I need to know what it was so we don't walk into the same trap.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde keeps her hand firm on Aldous's shoulder, steady as a ship's timber in rough water. She doesn't turn away from the black churning below, keeps her body between him and the rain as if that small shelter matters. Her voice stays low—a cook's voice, the one she uses when someone's breaking under pressure—but there's no kindness in it, only certainty. She's asking him to tell her about the Sunken Barge, about that chain, about what price the water wants from him. Because if that thing is coming for him, it might be coming for reasons she needs to understand.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: The water doesn't lie—whatever drags that chain is broken, driven to frenzy by what binds it. It's coming for us whether we cross or stand still.

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous's grip loosens on the rail as Ysolde's hand steadies him. He closes his eyes, feeling the rain hammer his face, and lets the chain-sound's pattern wash over him like he reads the rainfall itself—the omens in it clear as broken glass. His breath comes easier. When he opens his eyes again, certainty has replaced panic, and he speaks what the water has already told him.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: The bound ones in the water fear bright fire—help me set torches along every rail, or they drag themselves up here and take us all into the black water.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen strides to the railing and begins gathering everything combustible within reach—tarred rope, lamp oil from the Warden's post, anything that will feed flame. She wraps her cloak around one arm and starts laying out torches at intervals along the causeway's edge, her movements quick and practiced. She doesn't wait for permission. Whatever comes up that chain gets met with bright fire.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: We hold the line here. Everyone back from that rail—arm yourselves. Whatever comes dragging up that chain is ours to face.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire steps forward and positions herself between the churning water and the crowd, one hand settling on her weapon hilt. Her shoulders square, her weight balanced on the balls of her feet—the stance of someone who's held a gate, who knows what "the line" means. She keeps her eyes locked on the dark water where that chain-sound echoes, her jaw tight, her voice cutting clear through the rain like she's still wearing a badge.)

transcript.text:
Aldous's eyes snap fully open, rain-omens read clean at last — and what stumbles out of the dark toward the toll-post isn't the bound thing at all, but a Warden, half-collapsed against a piling, one hand clamped over a spear-wound leaking pink into the rain, the other still clutching her sealed patrol-slate like it's the only thing keeping her upright. "Chained... they're chained to the old cart-wreck at the Ford," she gasps to Aldous, recognizing something in his stance — old militia discipline, maybe, or just a face that isn't screaming. "Feral. Ignore steel, ignore pain. Only thing that turns them back is fire." Behind them, Morwen's line of torches catches one after another along the causeway rail, oil-slick tar going up in fat orange tongues that hiss against the downpour — Burning Brand Ready, a wall of light between the queue and the black water. Mire holds the crowd back from the rail with her badge-that-isn't-a-badge voice, and for one held breath the chain-drag out in the dark actually falters, like whatever wears it doesn't like what it's swimming toward.

The Warden's knees buckle; Aldous is the one who catches her.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: You're safe from that water now. Tell me what those things are and what you saw them fear.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde moves to support the Warden alongside Aldous, her hands steady against the bleeding wound. She speaks low and certain—the same voice she uses to calm panicking crew—asking questions in precise order to keep the woman focused on answers rather than pain. She draws out everything the Warden witnessed of the chained creatures in the water: their nature, their binding, what moves them and what breaks them.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: Easy—I have you. Don't go dark on me. What did you see at the Ford?

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous catches the Warden as her knees buckle, his grip iron-steady as he pulls her away from the rail's black edge and into the toll-post's shelter. Years under Captain Verrick have taught him the drill: purposeful, practiced, angling her weight to keep the bleeding from worsening. His eyes lock onto hers, watching for the glaze that means fading, and his voice cuts through the rain with the same certainty he reads into the rainfall itself. "You're safe. Tell me what found you.")

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: I am Morwen, Exorcist of Hollowmoot—by the old rites and the fire, you obey the light and return to the deep!

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen strides forward to the torch line, raising both arms, and speaks in a language older than the Order—syllables that carry weight and certainty. She doesn't plead or pray. She commands, her voice steady through the rain, riding the wall of orange flame like it's a weapon in her hands. The bound ones hesitated at fire once before; now she drives that hesitation into something deeper, something forced.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Steady now. I've got you. What's your patrol unit, and how many were you facing when that spear found you?

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire strides from her position at the crowd barrier toward Aldous and the collapsed Warden, keeping her body angled to shield both of them and maintain sight lines on the dark water. She kneels beside the Warden without flinching at the blood, her hands steady as a physician's as she assesses the spear-wound—depth, angle, whether the bleeding is manageable. Her voice cuts sharp and clear: the voice of someone still accustomed to command, to keeping people alive under pressure.)

transcript.text:
Ysolde's steady questions cut through the Warden's pain like a blade through rope — patiently, precisely, she draws out everything: the things at the Ford aren't drowned dead at all, but living folk dragged under by the hive and chained, deliberately, to the sunken cart-wreck by someone or something that wanted them kept there, kept close, kept hungry. "They don't come loose," the Warden — Toll-Keeper Ossa, her slate finally legible now that Aldous wipes the rain from it — rasps. "Chains rusted into the wreck's ribs. They just... strain toward the causeway every night the water rises." Understanding blooms clear and cold across the party: this isn't a hunting pack roaming free, it's something anchored, waiting, growing more desperate as the flood climbs.

Morwen doesn't wait for that understanding to finish landing. She turns to the black water and the failing chain-drag with both arms raised, voice pitched into the old Order rite, and drives the command home through the wall of fire her torches have built — *obey the light, return to the deep.* Out past the reeds, the dragging sound stutters, strains, and finally slackens, iron scraping to stillness against stone as whatever wears those chains sinks back rather than fight bright flame and an exorcist's true voice both. The queue exhales as one. Rain still hammers the causeway, the water is still a finger higher than an hour ago, but for tonight the bound ones have gone back under, and the toll-post holds. Ossa, bandaged and steadier now, presses her sealed slate into Aldous's hand — official warden's passage, no questions asked, for whoever pulled her out of the reeds. Somewhere south, past where the torchlight dies, the cart-wreck at Gullet Ford keeps its secret a little longer.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The causeway gives out into open channel a half-mile on, the rail dropping away into reeds taller than a man, and ahead the water narrows and quickens into the churn of Gullet Ford. Somewhere beneath that white water is the sunken cart, and the chains, and whoever the flood swallowed and never let go. The reeds press close on both banks — good cover for an ambush, better cover for something watching you cross. Ossa's slate buys you past any Warden checkpoint, but it won't hold back the current, and it won't answer for what's chained below.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: The cart's down there pulling at the water on the left—you can feel it if you know how to read a current. We cross the right channel where the water runs clear and fast. Watch for anything that doesn't move with the flood—that's what's hunting.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde moves to the rail where it gives way into open channel, her weight settling into the easy stance of someone who's spent half her life on river-barges. She stares down into the churn of Gullet Ford, reading the water the way she reads her crew—every ripple, every pull, every subtle drag in the current speaks to her of what lies below. Her fingers trace the air above the white water, following the hidden path around the sunken wreck. She's lived her life on rivers. She knows every channel, even the ones drowning in flood.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: The water speaks—there's a path through this ford if we read it right, but the current hides teeth. We move fast and keep fire burning, or we don't move at all.

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous steps to the edge where the causeway opens into reeds, rain-soaked and still. He stands motionless while the deluge hammers the dark water, his eyes tracking the current's rhythm around half-submerged reeds and broken stone. His hands open at his sides as if to catch and read the rainfall itself—watching where it breaks, where the current stutters, where the white churn of the ford hides depths. When he finally speaks, his voice carries the certainty of someone who's read an omen clean.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: The hive didn't chain them for cruelty—it chained them to hold them steady, to keep them hunting in place. Show me that wreck. I need to understand what's holding them before we cross.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen drives to the causeway's edge as the Ford's churn draws close, her eyes locked on the dark water below. She's reading the water the way she reads corruption—looking past the storm-spray for the iron-bound shadow of that sunken cart beneath, for the pattern of the chains and what they mean. Bound creatures don't frenzy without reason. Something willed this binding, and she means to know who and why before she walks past it.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Eyes open and weapons ready. These reeds are perfect cover—for them and for us. Let's move smart, not fast.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire steps to the fore of the group, her gaze sweeping across the reed-banks on both sides of the narrowing channel. She positions herself where she can watch both the water ahead and the party behind, her hand resting on her weapon's hilt, every sense tuned to catch movement or ripple in the reeds or churn of water that doesn't belong to the flood.)

transcript.text: Ysolde reads the ford like her own pulse, tracing the drag of current until the safe line reveals itself clean as a seam in cloth — hug the right channel, she says, where the water runs true and the cart's pull can't reach you. Aldous stares into the rain until the pattern breaks for him too, and between the two of them the party has more than a hunch now: a marked, known path through the white water, the reeds on either bank suddenly readable instead of just threatening. Morwen crouches at the reed-line and finds what she's looking for beneath the churn — the wreck, the rust-black chains, and the shape of something that hasn't broken free in a long time, straining but held, quieter than it should be. Mire keeps her back to the water and her eyes on the reeds, and nothing moves there that shouldn't — not yet. Between four sets of certain eyes, Gullet Ford stops being a wall of grey noise and becomes a crossing: a right-hand channel through clear water, chains that are holding for now, and reed-banks that, for this moment, are only watching, not hunting. The party doesn't need to gamble on the wreck at all — they thread the marked line and reach the far bank with the current at their backs, the sunken cart and its cargo of the drowned left straining uselessly behind them in the dark, and the reeds swallow them whole the moment their boots find mud on the far shore.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: Thom Cairnweaver was a reed-fisher who gave shelter to hive-touched refugees when the Wardens wanted them burned—he trusted me enough to risk everything for that shelter. I swore to him by the old rites that if the hive-sickness ever took his blood, I would come to him with mercy and the ancient words, not abandonment to the flames. He lived three years after that oath before the winter flood dragged him under. Now his widow Ess controls those nets, and she chooses the Wardens' fear over the faith Thom had in me.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: Ess! Thom bound these nets to me with oath-words—you're throwing away three years of trust because you're afraid. Cut them now, or I'm coming through, and we'll settle this the hard way when I reach you.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Mire was the one who took that girl. Three years back, doing Cartel work through the settlements—enforcing the order to burn the touched. Thom had been sheltering her in secret, a hive-touched refugee, only twelve years old. Mire chained her and delivered her to Cartel custody. The girl didn't come back alive. Ess watched it happen. She knows Mire's face, knows what she did, and she's blamed her every day since.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: I took that girl for the Cartel, and I've lived with that every day since. I won't ask you to forgive it. But I'm here to hold the line now, not break it—that has to count for something.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Mire accepts the compel on 'A Grieving Widow'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: The fisherfolk of the stilt-hut Morwen once called safe harbor rise from the reeds and pay out their nets and lines across the channel, boxing the party's boat in against the mud before anyone can speak a greeting. turns on the party, because A grieving widow has been sheltering in that same hut since the flood took her husband, and she's spent the day telling the family that every stranger who comes downriver drags the hive-curse with them — tonight she points a shaking finger at the party and the family believes her..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The reeds part all at once — not for the party, but around them. Fishing lines and weighted nets pay out from a dozen hidden poles, hissing taut across the channel until the boat rocks to a stop, hemmed in against the mud with nowhere to pole free. Lantern-light gutters up on the stilt-hut's porch, and there she is: Ess, Thom Cairnweaver's widow, thinner than Morwen remembers, a fishing spear held like it might still be a rite of its own. Behind her, sons and cousins and neighbors with hooks and gaff-poles crowd the rail, faces set the way frightened people's faces get right before they do something they'll regret. Ess doesn't raise her voice — she doesn't need to, over the rain and the creak of straining nets — she just lifts one shaking arm and points it straight at the boat. "That's them," she says to the family, not to the party. "Strangers off the flood road. You know what follows strangers."

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: Ess, I know you're terrified. Grief does that. But look at us—really look—and tell me: are we the ones you're actually afraid of?

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde steps to the front edge of the boat, hands open and empty, and meets Ess's eyes directly. She speaks with the calm certainty of someone who's held frightened people through storms—not pleading, not excusing, just truth spoken with the weight of a cook who listens to crew secrets. Her voice carries across the nets and rain, steady against the downpour.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: Your husband sheltered the cursed because he understood what you're forgetting: the flood speaks in chains, not in strangers' faces. Look at us, Ess. We're not carrying sickness—we're the crossing.

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous rises in the boat, rain streaming down his face, and steps deliberately toward the bow with hands open at his sides. The drowned-mark that clings to him—that shadow only visible in certain light—deepens as he moves into the lantern's reach. He's making himself visible, vulnerable, a target if they mean him one. He looks directly at Ess, not past her fear but straight through it.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: I was at Thom's side when the hive came for him, Ess, and I held it back. You know what I am—untouched by the sickness you fear. Cut these nets now, or I'm coming through.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen stands in the boat, rain streaming off her cloak, and speaks with the quiet certainty of someone untouched by the hive-sickness despite walking among the infected and dying. She doesn't shout. She names what Thom swore to her, invoking the old rites with a voice that cuts through fear and rain both like a blade through cord.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Ess. I see what you're doing, and I don't blame you—grief makes you do things. But these people didn't bring the flood. I did what I did, and I live with it every day. So you're going to let us through, or I'm coming through, and we both know how that ends.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire stands in the boat with her weapon hand resting on her hilt, shoulders squared, eyes locked on Ess across the water. She's not posturing or shouting—just clear, certain, the way someone stands when they've held a gate and understand what *the line* means. She lets the fisher-folk see that she's ready, that she understands what they're afraid of, and that she does not care. Some lines you hold even if it breaks you.)

transcript.text: Ysolde — overcome with Empathy: dice - - - -, invoking Exiled by the Stiltfolk Clans [YS-01] → Fair (+2) vs Fair (+2): TIE

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: I see it. I see what the nets took. But not now—the living need the crossing more than the dead need their words.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Aldous refuses the compel on 'Duty to the Dead'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Ess's voice cracks under Morwen's rite-words — the old rhythm lands like a blade through cord, and the widow staggers back a step against her own porch rail, one hand flying to her throat as if the sound itself struck her. Behind her the family wavers, hooks lowering an inch. Ysolde's plea buys a breath more of hesitation, though it costs her — a stray net-hook catches her forearm as the lines finally start to slacken, a shallow red line for her trouble, nothing worse. Then Mire steps forward into the lantern-light, weapon-hand steady on her hilt, and says the thing none of them expected: that she doesn't ask forgiveness, only asks to be let stand. Something in that — a hard-eyed woman naming her own guilt instead of denying it — breaks the family's nerve entirely. Nets go slack, poles are pulled back from the water, and one by one the Cairnweaver kin retreat up into the stilt-hut's shadow, leaving Ess alone at the rail with her shaking spear, no longer pointing at anyone. Aldous alone holds his ground on the dead — he won't let Thom's rites be his excuse to stall the living, not tonight, and he says so plainly, refusing the pull of duty. But grief and guilt aren't the only things the noise of nets and shouting drew through the reeds: torchlight flickers on the water downstream, and the unmistakable creak of poled boats reaches them — Cartel men, who know every hidden channel in this marsh, come to see what's tangled up their toll-water and who's making all the fuss. The stilt-hut standoff is over. A new one is already arriving.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: She was a neighbor from the settlements before I was exiled by the Kin—she remembered me when I was still part of something, and she knew about the mill because I told her, years back, when I was looking for a place the flood wouldn't find me.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: I know your face. I remember your kitchen-garden above the tide-line, before everything changed. We're going to get your family out, but I need to know: who else is still in that mill?

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Ysolde accepts the compel on 'An Abandoned Mill'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: A mother has been keeping her children dry for weeks in the grain loft of the Abandoned Mill — Ysolde's old childhood shelter from before her exile. Tonight she waded out through flooded, rotting halls to find the only person from the old days who might still listen to her. begs the party to go to She begs the party to carry word to the Order of the Dry Saint, whose priests hoard the last of the blight-cure lore — the only thing that might save her youngest, who's started humming the swarm-song in his sleep., because her son followed the swarm-song into the belltower.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The mill swallows what's left of the lantern-light the moment you step through its sagging doorway — stone walls that once kept grain dry now hold nothing but black water and the smell of rot. Up in the loft, wedged above the flood line on planks that groan with every shift of weight, a woman named Sela crouches over two younger children, a third space beside her conspicuously, terribly empty. She knows Ysolde's face before she knows what to say to it — old neighbor, old kindness, the only name from before the exile she trusted enough to wade through rotten halls searching for. Her youngest followed the swarm-song three nights ago, out past where the belltower's drowned bell still somehow rings, and now the two children left to her have started humming in their sleep. She doesn't ask you to save him. She asks you to reach the Order of the Dry Saint before the humming becomes something worse — they hoard the only cure-lore left in the Sallowmere, and Hollowmoot is far, and the water is rising a finger an hour.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: I remember your kitchen-garden, Sela, before everything broke—your son's humming the deep-song, which means we're running toward help that exists, not away from the Wardens. Tell me his name, and I swear by the reed-channels that won't shelter me: we will reach Hollowmoot and get the cure-lore.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde moves to Sela without hesitation and takes her shoulders, meeting her eyes with the steady certainty of someone who's guided fractured crews through chaos before. She's already reading the water level below, already thinking of the mill's highest stone walls as refuge. She turns to the party with the precise, unhurried movements of a night-barge cook in a storm and gestures them to gather what can be carried—her focus already shifting toward the loft's edge, ready to move them all out before the approaching Cartel boats reach the flooded doors.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: The swarm is only testing them—not yet deep rooted. The Order's cure-lore is real, but it demands what the Order always demands: truth paid in the old way. We reach Hollowmoot with words they'll listen to, or we don't reach them at all.

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous settles beside the humming children in the grain loft, listening to that thin sound the way he reads an omen in falling rain. His hands open at his sides, not touching—just sensing the arc of the hive-sickness as it traces through small bodies. He's walked between the drowned and the living; he knows the difference between a curse taking hold and one merely testing its grip. His eyes meet Sela's when he stands again, steady and certain.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: The swarm-song isn't calling to them blind—it wants something specific. Tell me what your son heard first, what drew him into that belltower, and I'll know what we're dealing with before we run.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen steps close to the two children, studying them the way an exorcist reads corruption—watching where the infection sits, how it moves through breath and blood-sound, what it wants from them. She's untouched by the hive, so she can see it clearly in others, trace its pattern like iron in cord. Her attention is absolute as she asks Sela about the eldest child, about the moment he heard it, about what the swarm-song promised him. This is the work of someone taking the measure of a thing before she decides how to cut it out.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Cartel's got the routes memorized, and they'll be in bow range in minutes. I need to count heads and read what they want before we promise this woman anything we can't deliver.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire moves to the mill's highest window, her militia training automatic. She reads the approaching torchlight the way she read Gullet Ford—counting the boats and men, gauging their speed and bearing against the current. Each detail speaks: how many oars, who's armed with what, whether they're coming to investigate a noise or coming to collect. She positions herself where she can watch both the water-approach and the mill's interior exits, shoulders squared the way someone stands when they know the line is about to be tested.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: That's Thresh calling me across the water. He's come to collect, and now we're all in his sights—which means we move now, or we don't move at all.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Mire accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Aldous — create advantage with Lore: dice - 0 + 0 → Good (+3) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Morwen — create advantage with Lore: dice + 0 - + → Great (+4) vs Poor (-1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Mire — create advantage with Notice: dice 0 - + + → Great (+4) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Aldous reads the boy's absence the way he reads storm-omens, and what he finds is almost mercy: the swarm-song is testing, not yet rooted — a claim laid on the boy, not a chain sunk in. There may still be time, if the party moves fast and true. Morwen goes further, tracing the shape of the infection through the two remaining children like iron laid in cord, and understands its rhythm now — it wants to be *answered*, not merely heard, which means the Order's lore isn't just a cure, it might be a counter-song. At the window, Mire counts torches on the black water and her breath goes short: she knows those oars, that lean-forward stance at the tiller. "Thresh," she says, flat. Cartel muscle, come to collect what she owes, and he's brought enough men that this isn't a friendly toll-stop — three boats, hooked spears glinting wet in the lantern-light, closing on the mill with the unhurried confidence of men who already know there's nowhere for the party to run. Sela clutches her two remaining children tighter at the sound of Mire's voice cracking on that name, understanding without being told that the strangers who came to save her son have brought trouble of their own to her door. The mill's rotten floorboards groan under six sets of shifting weight as the choice crystallizes: stand here and answer Thresh now, or slip out the flood-side door with Sela's plea in hand and outrun him toward Hollowmoot.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Thresh doesn't shout orders — he doesn't need to. His three boats fan out to cover both the water approach and the flood-side door, hooked spears held low and ready, men settling into the patient, unhurried postures of collectors who've done this a hundred times. He stands in the prow of the lead boat, rain sheeting off a wide-brimmed hat, and calls Mire's name across the water like an old debt finally come due — not a threat yet, just a fact. Behind the party, Sela pulls her remaining children deeper into the loft's shadow, torn between the strangers who promised to save her son and the trouble they've dragged to her door. The mill's rotten floor gives them maybe thirty seconds before those spears start closing the gap for real.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: Sela, we move now, while his attention is still on the porch. I know this mill's water like breath. There's a way through.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde moves to Sela without hesitation, reading the water-pressure outside like she reads a crew in a storm — quick, certain, no waste. She guides them toward the flood-side door, one hand on the mother's shoulder, voice low and steady. "There's a channel behind the east buttress, the one his boats missed. The current runs fast there. We move now." She's already moving them, already seeing the route only someone who knows these waters *as kin* would find.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: The rain carries your name, Thresh, and what follows it—a collector who speaks in coin still, not blood. That's a choice you've made. Let's talk price before it changes.

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous steps forward from the mill's shadow into the rain-light, placing himself visibly between Mire and the water-approach. He moves with deliberate slowness, reading Thresh's posture and voice the way he reads omens in falling rain — and what he reads is a man who came to collect coin, not blood. Not yet. He makes himself a target and a negotiation point, rain streaming down his face as he meets Thresh across the dark water.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: Thresh! You've come for Mire's debt, but this child carries the swarm-song—and that's MY domain now, not the Cartel's. Walk back those boats, or I'll give you a reason that doesn't involve coin.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen steps to the mill door's edge, visible to Thresh across the black water, and plants herself as the direct obstacle to his approach. She's untouched by the hive-sickness, known by name throughout the Sallowmere—and she's making it clear she's not a target to be pushed around. She stands with the absolute certainty of someone who's walked among the infected and lived, and she's challenging him to move past her.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Thresh. You came for me, and I'm right here. The debt is mine—but these people aren't part of what I owe you.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire steps into the window frame where Thresh can see her clearly, rain streaming down her face. She stands with the hard-won certainty of someone who's held a gate—shoulders squared, weapon hand steady, eyes locked on Thresh across the dark water. She makes it personal, makes it clear: if he wants payment, it's here, it's her, and nothing between him and the mill's other occupants matters as much as what stands between her and him.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Ysolde — overcome with Contacts: dice 0 - 0 +, invoking Knows every hidden channel [YS-01] → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Morwen — attack with Will: dice - + - - → Fair (+2) vs Superb (+5): SUCCESS MAJOR COST (Thresh stress 1)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Mire — create advantage with Provoke: dice 0 0 - -, invoking Owes blood-debt to the Cartel [MI-03], Still fights like she's badged [MI-04] → Great (+4) vs Superb (+5): SUCCESS MAJOR COST

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Thresh attacks Mire (physical): Fair (+2) vs Mire's Athletics Fair (+2) — defended

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Morwen's rite-words land like a blow — Thresh staggers, breath punched out of him — but the flood outside answers her voice with a surge of its own. The channel Ysolde marked behind the east buttress swells and swallows itself whole, boiling brown water where clear current ran a moment ago: the escape route is gone, at least by boat, and now the only ways out of this are through Thresh's men or up into water no one can outrun.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Mire plants her feet to bait Thresh, weapon-hand steady, voice carrying — and it works, his attention locks on her, the taunt landing exactly as she meant it to. But the mill's grain-loft floor was never built on pilings; away from the old supports the rotten boards flex and give like sodden reed-mat over black mud, and her back foot punches half through the wood, leg wedged and exposed right as Thresh's spearmen mark her as the clear, unmoving target.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text:
Ysolde doesn't wait for the water to decide anything — she reads Sela's whole body already, the fear cording her shoulders, and simply chooses another way: not the drowned channel but the mill's own bones, the halls she ran through as a girl. She has Sela and the two children moving through a service passage behind the grain hoist before anyone else has finished shouting, boots splashing through ankle-deep flood but clear of Thresh's spears entirely — a route none of his men know because it was never a smuggler's route, only a child's. Above the water, Morwen's rite-word finally lands true, and Thresh folds around the blow, breath gone from him in one ragged grunt — but the marsh itself answers her voice like it's listening, and the current behind the east buttress boils and rises and swallows the escape channel whole, closing the one clean way out by boat. Mire's taunt does exactly what she wanted — Thresh's eyes lock on her and nowhere else — but the loft floor was never meant to hold like the pilings below, and her back leg punches through rotten planking up to the knee, pinning her half a step from the window, plainly, helplessly visible. Thresh barks the order without hesitation, two spears arcing low across the black water for the woman wedged in his sightline — but Mire wrenches sideways even trapped, weapon-hand coming up fast enough to knock one shaft wide and let the second bury itself in the sill inches from her ribs instead of in her.

The mill groans around them all: Sela's family vanishing down a passage only Ysolde could have found, Thresh straightening slow and furious in his boat with Morwen's blow still ringing in his chest, and Mire fighting her own trapped leg while his spearmen realize their first throw missed and start closing the range for a second.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: Sela, upper rooms on the south side. Get as high as you can—and stay there.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde guides Sela and the two children up the narrow stone stairs, checking windows as she goes to make sure there's a roof-way out if the water keeps climbing. Then she's moving back down into the flooded passages, boots splashing through ankle-deep water, reading the pressure of it against the mill's old bones like she reads the pulse of a crew in a storm. She knows how floodwater moves through drowned halls—where it presses, where it swells, which pillars weaken under the surge. Up in the loft, her crew is out of time. Down here, the rising water has its own currents, and she knows every one of them.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: I've got you—the rain reads their angle. We move NOW.

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous lunges for the window, grabbing Mire's arm to help wrench her trapped leg free from the splintered boards. He reads the falling rain for the angle and rhythm of the approaching spears, then pulls her back from the sill toward the deeper mill interior, away from the targeting line.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: Your men stand down, Cartel man. Your debt is with Mire alone—call them back now, or I'll teach you what it means when an exorcist stops playing defense.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen strides fully into the mill doorway, rite-words building in her throat like pressure in the air. She plants herself between Thresh and Mire, untouched by the swarm-song and armored in something deeper than flesh, and hurls her will at him—old words, old power meant to unmake worse things than Cartel muscle.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Come on then, Thresh. You've got her family running. Let's finish what you came for—me.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire braces both hands on the solid window sill and hauls hard, tendons straining as she wrenches her leg free from the splintered, sodden floorboards. Pain lances through her calf where the wood tore skin—she's bleeding freely into the rain—but the pin releases. She comes up into a fighting stance in the window frame, weight balanced, weapon-hand steady despite everything. Now she's mobile. Now Thresh has to come through her to reach anyone else in this mill.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: The rain reads your angle clear—you're coming up and OUT. Stay with me!

transcript.text: Aldous gets Mire moving, but the flooded floor itself fights him for her — the same sucking black mud that ate the loft's pilings grabs at his boots as he hauls her back from the sill, and the drag costs them the last clear seconds: by the time he wrenches free, Thresh's spearmen have closed half the distance to the doorway.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text:
The mud wins its inch and then loses the fight — Aldous curses, hauls one boot free with a wet tearing sound, then the other, dragging Mire the last stride from the sill even as the sucking black floor claws at both of them. It costs precious seconds: Thresh's spearmen close half the gap to the doorway, hooked points lowering, close enough now that the next throw won't miss high.

But Morwen isn't done. Her second rite-word lands harder than the first, old syllables cracking across the water like a whip — Thresh doubles over in the prow of his boat, one hand white-knuckled on the gunwale, breath sawing wet and ragged. He's hurt now, really hurt, and for the first time since he called Mire's name across the flood, something like doubt crosses his face. Mire doesn't let him recover it — she comes up out of the window frame fully mobile, blood-streaked leg and all, weapon drawn, plainly ready to make the next exchange cost him men he can't easily replace. Behind them all, Ysolde has already read the mill's bones perfectly: Sela and the children are tucked high and dry, the service passage sealed at her back, the route she knows holding steady even as the boat-channel outside stays drowned.

Thresh straightens slow, one hand pressed to his ribs, and does the arithmetic every Cartel man does in the end — a wounded collector, a debt that isn't worth dying for tonight, spearmen who'll want hazard pay for a fight that's already gone sideways twice. He spits into the black water, calls off the second throw with a sharp gesture, and orders the boats back into the reeds, promising Mire in a voice gone thin with pain that this isn't finished, that the debt doesn't drown with the mill. The torches recede downstream. The mill goes quiet except for rain and the groan of rotten timber, and somewhere above, Sela's children have stopped humming — for now.

ambiguities.issue: Tension was reduced by 1 at scene end (event 33, notes 'resolved -1') for 'the party resolved a THREAT,' but no clock_change was ever logged against T-01 in this scene, and no roll against it was logged as Success With Style on an overcome action or a 'taken out' result (the SWS rolls that occurred were Create Advantage, not Overcome/Attack-taken-out; the one Attack roll against T-01, event 32, was a plain success, shifts 2). ambiguities.issue: The Story Pile draw for the 'success with style on create an advantage' trigger (rail_add PS-02 at event 20, story_draw at event 21) is logged BEFORE the triggering roll itself resolves (event 22). ambiguities.section: §3 (Outcomes and deck draws table) / standard Fate Create Advantage rules
ambiguities.issue: Three of the four rolls this scene (events 43, 45, 48) are Create Advantage actions that hit success-with-style (3+ shifts). The spec's SWS row says the player 'may look at the top card of the Session Deck... instead of taking a boost.' In baseline Fate, a boost is the SWS reward for Overcome/Attack; Create Advantage's normal SWS reward is a full aspect with 2 free invokes, not a boost. The log shows the actors receiving BOTH the deck peek (events 44, 46, 49) AND the standard 2 free invokes on the created aspect (notes: '2 free'), so it's unclear whether the peek is meant to replace the 2-free-invoke CA bonus, stack with it, or simply not apply to Create Advantage rolls at all.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The table treated the deck-peek as an additional bonus stacked on top of the normal 2-free-invoke Create Advantage reward, since no explicit rule denies it.

ambiguities.section: §7 (Scene loop, cleanup step 5) and §5 (Beat Frame procedure)
ambiguities.issue: Cleanup step 5 says to 'Deploy each one [trigger] that fired' during the current scene's cleanup, but the log shows module trigger M-1 and Beat Frame trigger B-03 marked only as 'fired' (events 52-53) with no immediate deployment (no card draws, no rail placement, no frame sentence read) before scene end. B-03's note 'scene_start:3' implies deployment is deferred to the start of scene 3 rather than executed in scene 2's cleanup as the text seems to require.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Treated 'deploy' as meaning the trigger is queued and its effects (Beat Frame reading, module reveal) manifest at the opening of the next scene, rather than requiring immediate on-the-spot deployment inside the current scene's cleanup step.

ambiguities.issue: The spec defines a backup module only as '2 GM cards clipped together, plus one trigger' but never specifies the mechanical deployment procedure (e.g., do the two cards go face-up on the rail immediately? Do they enter the Session Deck? Is a draw made?) the way §5 spells out for Beat Frames. When M-1 fired (event 52) there was no defined procedure to follow.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: No deployment event was logged for M-1 in this scene; the table appears to have deferred/no-op'd module deployment pending a defined procedure.

ambiguities.section: §3 Free invokes from cards / rail rules
ambiguities.issue: GM card C-02 is invoked twice in the scene on two different tags ('ash marks on doors' at event 74 and 'neighbours inform on neighbours' at event 75), but a face-up GM card only grants 1 free invoke total per scene. The log's fp_spent field only tracks the rolling player's spend, so it's impossible to tell whether the GM paid a fate point for the second invoke (which would be legal, since any face-up tag is invokable for a fate point) or whether the GM used two 'free' invokes off one card (which would not be legal).
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Treated as compliant on the assumption the GM's second invoke on C-02 was paid from the GM's own fate point pool, since the log format does not separately record GM fate-point expenditure.

ambiguities.section: §4 Resolving a drawn player card / §3 outcomes table (tie)
ambiguities.issue: The tie draw (PX-22, event 73) occurred during Ysolde's roll (event 74), but the resulting compel to the card's owner (Aldous) was not delivered until event 78, after two other players' full rolls (events 75-76) and a peek (event 77) had already resolved. The rules specify what a drawn player card compel must contain, but not how promptly it must be offered relative to other actions in the scene.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Treated as acceptable since the compel was still delivered within the same scene before cleanup; the table allowed other declared actions to resolve first.

ambiguities.issue: Tension was lowered by 1 (event 82, 'resolved -1'), which per the table requires 'The party resolved a THREAT or filled a player's goal.' No THREAT or FACTION card is shown being taken out or having its clock filled this scene; C-02 was merely discarded for rail-limit reasons (event 79), not resolved. It's unclear whether the GM instead counted the successful social resolution of the framed scene question (getting past Ess/the family) as 'filled a player's goal' under this rule.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Accepted the GM's -1 adjustment on the reading that successfully talking the party past the stilt-hut family, tied to Morwen's and Mire's personal goals, counts as 'filled a player's goal.'

ambiguities.section: §4 Resolving a drawn player card, step 2
ambiguities.issue: Two of the three drawn-player-card compels this scene (PX-09 'nets and fishing lines' at event 61, and PX-22 'guards the drowned bodies' at event 78) used a power tag instead of the default weakness tag. The rule permits this only if the power tag 'causes the trouble directly.' Both are plausible readings but borderline, and the spec gives only one worked example to calibrate against.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Both power-tag compels were accepted as valid under the 'causes trouble directly' exception, since in each case the named power tag was the literal mechanism of the complication (nets physically restraining the boat; drawn-to-the-body compulsion causing the delay).

ambiguities.section: §4 (Resolving a drawn GM card) vs §5 (Beat Frame procedure)
ambiguities.issue: §5's Beat Frame procedure only describes how player cards surface/compel (step 6, citing §4) but never says whether a GM-owned card drawn to fill an open blank (here F-02, a FACTION card filling WHERE) goes face-up with the GM free invoke as in §4's 'Resolving a drawn GM card.' The log placed F-02 on the rail (event 93) without logging a free invoke note, unlike PX-04's explicit '1 free invoke(s)' note (event 96).
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Table treated the GM card as resolved per §4's GM-card procedure (face-up, GM builds the twist from its tags) but did not explicitly log a free invoke grant, creating inconsistent record-keeping rather than a clear rule violation.

ambiguities.issue: Tension dropped 2->1 (event 110) citing 'resolved' outcome, but no logged event shows a THREAT/FACTION being resolved, a clock filling, or a player goal being explicitly closed out (F-02's clock stayed at 0/5, untouched). The only relevant activity was three create-advantage rolls and a compel.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: GM appears to have judged that the create-advantage successes against Sela/the FACTION effectively 'filled a player's goal' (helping Sela) even though this isn't captured as a discrete loggable trigger; treated as sufficient to apply -1.

ambiguities.issue: The event log has no field for GM fate-point expenditure. GM tags on face-up card T-03 are invoked twice within scene 5 (event 125: 'hooked spears and cudgels'; event 129: 'take hostages for leverage'), but the rule grants only 1 free invoke per face-up GM card 'to be used within that scene,' and no rail_add event shows T-03 being freshly placed face-up this scene (it appears to already be on the rail from an earlier scene, so no new free invoke should have been generated). Whether the second invoke was a paid GM fate-point spend or an improper reuse of the single free invoke cannot be determined from the log as structured.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Treated the second invoke of T-03 as a paid invoke drawn from the GM's per-scene fate point budget, since the log records no explicit denial and the engine did not flag a refusal.

ambiguities.section: §3 (Outcomes and deck draws) / §4 (When the deck runs out)

friction.text: Story Pile draw for the SWS-create-advantage trigger (PS-02) fired before the triggering roll resolved (events 20-21 precede event 22), an ordering problem the spec's 'no draw except on listed Fate events' language doesn't anticipate.

Aldous received both the Story Pile ally (PS-02, event 22) AND a separate Session Deck peek (H-04, event 23) off the same single success-with-style result, double-dipping a reward §6A explicitly frames as an either/or substitution.

A compel's fictional complication (event 11) was fully authored before the Story Pile draw it triggered (PS-13, events 12-13) was even revealed, so the rule that the complication 'must involve' the drawn card couldn't meaningfully be honored - the deck-draw discipline that is supposed to be 'the point of the system' quietly slipped here.
Backup modules have a trigger but no defined deployment procedure (unlike Beat Frames' explicit draw-and-fill steps in §5), so when M-1 fired it was unclear what mechanically should happen next.

The SWS 'peek instead of a boost' option collides with standard Fate's separate 2-free-invoke reward for Create Advantage successes with style, and the spec never clarifies whether these stack, replace each other, or whether the peek option even applies to Create Advantage rolls at all — this came up 3 times in one scene.
The Tension +1 'fled/bypassed' adjustment (event 50) cites no specific face-up THREAT/FACTION card in the log, making it hard to verify against the §6 table's actual trigger condition.

Refusal handling: §4 mandates a GM-tag-based cost when a player refuses a deck-draw compel, but the log shows no explicit application of that cost after Aldous's refusal — only an incidental Beat Frame trigger, which is a different mechanism.

The log format doesn't separately capture GM fate-point spends, making it impossible to verify compliance with the 'one free invoke per face-up GM card' cap when a GM card's tag is invoked more than once in a scene.

Judgment calls on power-tag vs. weakness-tag compels (the 'causes trouble directly' exception in §4 step 2) recur and are decided case-by-case with no crisper test in the spec, making consistency across the table hard to enforce.

Story Pile draw (PS-17) triggered correctly by the mechanics but left mechanically and narratively inert — never invoked, never tied to the compel it supposedly resulted from, wasting the §6A free-invoke grant and the card's presence on the rail.

Inconsistent logging of GM free invokes: player card surfacing (PX-04) explicitly notes '1 free invoke(s)' while the GM FACTION card (F-02) filling a Beat Frame blank gets no equivalent note, making it hard to audit whether the GM actually received/used its §4 free invoke.
The tension drop to 1 (event 110) is not traceable to any single logged trigger from the §6 adjustment table, making tension-track auditing difficult from the event log alone.

Draw events (e.g., 124, 127) are logged before the roll events that trigger them (125, 129), making it hard to audit causal order (roll result -> chosen cost tier -> draw) directly from the log sequence.

The log schema has no field for GM fate-point spends, so repeated invokes of a face-up GM card's tags within one scene (T-03 invoked twice, events 125 and 129) cannot be verified against the '1 free invoke per face-up card' rule (§3).

The deck-exhaustion edge case is only partially resolved: an interim ruling covers ties/costs using face-up GM tags (AMB-16), but the success-with-style 'peek' option's behavior with an empty deck (event 142) is left unaddressed by any rule or ruling.

free_text.best_moment: Guiding Sela and the children through the mill's hidden service passages. That moment crystallized what makes Ysolde work: her exile history became immediately personal, her knowledge of river-ways and buildings translated to actual survival, and a family was saved because only she knew the hidden route. It felt like Ysolde's specific skills and past were essential.
free_text.most_frustrating: Nothing major - the session had excellent pacing and tension. Smallest note: would have liked more mechanical use of Ysolde's heretic status and Order-cipher knowledge. Also could have pushed the exile dynamic with Ess deeper into personal confrontation rather than just negotiation.
free_text.background_used: Very well. Sela's recognition from before the exile, the mill as Ysolde's childhood shelter, and river-reading as core survival mechanics were woven in organically from questions the GM asked. The exile complication with Ess added necessary texture. Only note: the exile's weight could have created sharper mechanical tension or advantage.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Use the Order-cipher knowledge and heretic aspects more mechanically. Would've liked to probe why Ysolde's exile happened and what it means to someone like Sela who still remembers her fondly - that emotional geography could have deepened the personal stakes.
free_text.one_sentence: The mill connection and exile complications with Ess and Sela felt organic and excellent, creating real stakes that mattered to Ysolde personally; the heretic and scholar aspects stayed dormant, but this was the right story to spotlight Ysolde the river-wise outsider.

free_text.best_moment: When Aldous stepped into the rain in front of Thresh and read him as a collector who still spoke in coin, not blood yet—it felt like stepping into danger for someone else (Mire) and actually using my core ability (reading omens in rainfall) to de-escalate instead of fight. The character's priorities showed: safety first, reading second.
free_text.most_frustrating: The escape channel collapsing exactly when we needed it felt slightly railroaded—I understand it created dramatic tension, but it removed the clean option right as we'd planned it. Also wanted more time to engage with the swarm-song mystery itself rather than just running from Thresh.
free_text.background_used: Heavily and well. The Sunken Barge panic got invoked as a real complication (compel at the causeway), my ferryman's vow drove my actions with Sela, reading rainfall was mechanically central to multiple scenes, and Captain Verrick's discipline came up organically when catching Ossa. None of it felt forced—it all complicated what I was trying to do.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to actually help Sela's son—to engage with the hive-sickness lore directly instead of just running away from it. The scene setup made that impossible (Thresh's arrival forced the choice), which is dramatically sound but left that thread hanging for me narratively.
free_text.one_sentence: The backstory was used as real constraint and complication rather than just flavor, which made every choice matter—panic near water, duty to carry souls, inability to lie to the Order—these were tested, not just acknowledged.

free_text.best_moment: Standing in the mill doorway and speaking rite-words that actually made Thresh double over—that was the exorcist power fantasy working exactly right, untouched and dangerous and exactly what I built her to be.
free_text.most_frustrating: The flood surge that closed off Ysolde's escape route right after I challenged Thresh felt like circumstances conspiring to lock me into a direct fight rather than leaving me tactical options.
free_text.background_used: Yes—Thom's oath to shelter hive-touched became the emotional core of the Ess confrontation, and my exorcist identity was validated repeatedly. It landed well: created immediate stakes and made me the character who could perceive and answer hive-corruption where others just feared it.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted more time to read and understand the swarm-song infection through Sela's children before Thresh interrupted—that scene got cut short. Also would have liked a longer negotiation with Thresh rather than escalating straight to rite-word confrontation.
free_text.one_sentence: My backstory felt used well—the oath to Thom, my untouched status, my exorcist role—all became central to the drama instead of window-dressing.

free_text.best_moment: The mill window confrontation with Thresh—the visceral moment of being wedged in the loft, taking a spear meant to kill me, then wrenching my own leg free and coming up bloody but ready to fight. It distilled everything Mire is: the hard-won competence, the willingness to take the hit, the refusal to step back.
free_text.most_frustrating: The environmental hazards stacking faster than I could respond to them—the floor collapsing under me during my provocation, the escape channel boiling closed right after I committed to the conversation with Thresh. I felt cornered by circumstances rather than shaped by my own choices. Less "the GM was unfair" and more "I wanted to make a plan and execute it, but the water had other ideas."
free_text.background_used: Very well—the girl I took for the Cartel became Ess's recognition and blame, the Cartel debt became Thresh, my militia training shaped how I held every line. None of it felt forced; it all felt like the GM saying "I see who this person is, and I'm going to make her reckon with it." The compel on "A Grieving Widow" was the sharpest moment: Ess knew my face. That hit different.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted a longer moment with Ess at the stilt-hut—to do more than make a hard statement about living with guilt. The other PCs' rolls resolved the tension before I could really *engage* with her accusation. I also would have liked one clear choice about how to escape the mill rather than reacting to each crisis as it collapsed around me.
free_text.one_sentence: Used well—my past wasn't wielded against me unfairly, but it was wielded directly and often, leaving me constantly choosing between my old debts and new loyalties, which is exactly what Mire's character needed.
